title: Duke's copyists and sight-reading three trombone parts
summary: He explains how Ellington's compact scores worked and recalls a sight-read piece for three trombones.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Did Duke copy his own music?
And the copyist had to know his style — because he might just give you two staff lines for the whole band sometimes, or three maybe. And you had to know, like a guy named © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
Tom Whaling did it for many years, Chuck Conners did it for a little bit and Joe Benjamin, the bass player.
So they actually scored some of his — I mean he wouldn’t write the whole score.
He would, but he had a way to do it, really compact.
Oh all the notes were there.
Oh, okay. And they had to sort them out.

Even one night Duke had three trombones, one line with all three parts, but it was like — and we sight read it on a concert. And it went okay. You know it was some kind of piece, ahh, after he read Hailie Selassie, it was about the lion of Judah, or the name of the lion that met us at the airport, it was some messianic, or, I can’t remember, my friend will remember, and he was writing this song about it. So we got through it and Duke said, “Ladies and gentlemen, I’d like you to meet three of the most courageous trombone players you’ll ever meet.”
